sub: Named after “man” (al-insān) in ayah 1; also called Ad-Dahr, “time”
theme: Man was once nothing, then was created and tested with a clear choice: gratitude or ingratitude. The surah shows where each path ends, and dwells at length on the reward of the righteous.
story: Reports differ on where it came down. Many place it early in Makkah; others say Madinah, or Makkah with a few Madinan ayat. The Prophet ﷺ used to recite it, with As-Sajdah, in the Fajr prayer on Fridays.
It reminds man that he was once nothing, then was made from a drop, given hearing and sight, and shown the way. The test is simple: will he be grateful or ungrateful?

One ayah covers the deniers’ fate; eighteen describe the reward of the righteous and the deeds that earned it. Then the Prophet ﷺ is told to be patient, worship day and night, and never give in to the deniers, who love this passing world.

sections.title: Man made from a drop to be tested: grateful or ungrateful
sections.meaning: There was a long time when man was nothing worth mentioning. Allah made him from a mixed drop in order to test him, gave him hearing and sight, and showed him the way. Now the choice is his: grateful or ungrateful.
points: Man was once nothing worth mentioning
Made from a mixed drop to be tested; given hearing and sight
Shown the way: grateful or ungrateful
sections.matters: It sets up the whole surah: everything after it shows where the two choices lead. It also humbles man. The one who was nothing yesterday has no reason to be arrogant today.
sections.story: No specific incident. It opens by reminding man of his beginning, to set up the test that the rest of the surah follows.
explained: Hal atā asks a question whose answer is obvious: yes. There was a long stretch of time when man was nothing anyone mentioned, either Adam as a form of clay before the soul, or each of us before and in the womb.

Then Allah made him from nuṭfah amshāj, a drop mixed from man and woman, changing stage by stage. The point is a test, so He gave him hearing and sight and made both paths clear. Man becomes either shākir or kafūr.
teaches: Remember you were once nothing, and stay humble.
Your hearing and sight were given to you for a test.
Allah made the way clear; the choice is yours.
Gratitude is the path of faith.
sections.hook: The shortest section, three ayat. Al-insān is named in 1 and 2, and ayah 3 ends on the two options, shākir or kafūr. Keep as-sabīl (3) in mind: it returns in ayah 29.

sections.title: Chains for deniers; camphor cups for the righteous who fed the poor
sections.meaning: The deniers get chains, collars and a blaze. The righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, from a spring they direct at will. Why? They kept their vows, feared the Day, and fed the poor, the orphan and the captive for Allah alone. So Allah shielded them and rewarded their patience.
points: Chains, collars and a blaze for the disbelievers
The righteous drink a camphor-mixed cup from a gushing spring
They keep vows and fear a Day of spreading evil
They feed others for Allah alone, wanting no thanks
Shielded from that Day; radiance, joy, a garden and silk
sections.matters: It shows that Paradise is earned by real deeds: keeping promises, feeding people who can give nothing back, and doing it only for Allah. The warning takes one ayah; hope fills the rest.
sections.story: Reports differ on ayat 8–9. They are tied to an Anṣārī family who fed three hungry people, to those who cared for the captives of Badr, or to ʿAlī and Fāṭimah, in a story judged weak. The ayat cover all the righteous.
explained: After one short ayah on chains, collars and a blazing Fire, the focus turns to al-abrār, the righteous. They drink a cup mixed with kāfūr, cool and fragrant, from a spring they can make flow wherever they wish.

Their deeds: they keep their vows and fear a Day whose evil spreads everywhere. They give food they love to the poor, the orphan and the captive, seeking only Allah’s face, not thanks. So Allah shields them, lights up their faces, fills their hearts with joy, and rewards their patience with a garden and silk.
teaches: Keep your promises, especially those made to Allah.
Give what you love, not just leftovers.
Do good for Allah, not for thanks or praise.
Fear of that Day drives good deeds.
sections.hook: Sharr links it: they fear a Day whose sharr spreads (7), and Allah shields them from the sharr of that Day (11). Kāfūr (5) echoes kafūr at the end of ayah 3.

sections.title: Paradise up close: couches, silver cups, Salsabīl, silk; their effort appreciated
sections.meaning: Paradise up close: couches with no heat or cold, shade and fruit within reach, silver cups clear as glass, a ginger-mixed drink from the spring Salsabīl, ageless servants like scattered pearls, green silk and silver bracelets. Then the best part: “Your effort has been appreciated.”
points: Couches, no sun or cold; shade and fruit close at hand
Silver vessels clear as glass, measured just right
A ginger-mixed cup from the spring Salsabīl
Ageless youths like scattered pearls; a great kingdom
Green silk, silver bracelets, a pure drink from their Lord
This is your reward; your effort is appreciated
sections.matters: Section 2 named the reward; this section lets you picture it. It ends with words of appreciation from Allah Himself, which make every small effort in this life worth it.
sections.story: Reportedly, an Abyssinian man was with the Prophet ﷺ when this was revealed. Hearing Paradise described, he asked if his eyes would see what the Prophet’s ﷺ eyes would see there. Told yes, he wept until he died. The Prophet ﷺ recited ayah 22 at his grave.
explained: The righteous recline on couches under canopies. There is no scorching sun and no bitter cold. Shade is close, and fruit lowers itself to them whether they stand, sit or lie down. Servants bring silver vessels that are somehow clear as glass, filled to exactly the amount they want.

They drink a ginger-mixed cup from the spring Salsabīl. Ageless youths serve them like scattered pearls, and everywhere is bliss and a vast kingdom. They wear green silk and silver bracelets, and their Lord gives them a pure drink that cleans the heart. Then the honour: “This is your reward; your effort is appreciated.”
teaches: Nothing in Paradise harms or tires you.
What Allah prepares is beyond anything in this world.
A pure heart is part of Paradise’s reward.
sections.hook: Silver shines three times: vessels (15), qawārīr min fiḍḍah (16), bracelets (21). Qawārīr ends 15 and opens 16. The ginger cup and spring (17–18) mirror the camphor cup and spring (5–6).

sections.title: Quran sent in stages: be patient and pray; deniers love this world
sections.meaning: Allah Himself sent the Quran down in stages. So the Prophet ﷺ must be patient, obey no sinner or denier, and remember Allah morning, evening and through the night. The deniers love this passing world, yet Allah made them and can replace them. This is a reminder, but no one wills unless Allah wills.
points: We sent the Quran down to you, in stages
Be patient; obey no sinner or denier
Remember Allah morning and evening; prostrate and glorify at night
They love this world; We made them and can replace them
A reminder; you will only if Allah wills; mercy or punishment
sections.matters: It turns from the reward to the one carrying the message. Its answer to pressure and opposition is patience plus worship, day and night. It ends by putting the choice back to each person, within Allah’s will.
sections.story: Makkah’s leaders tried threats and bribes. Reportedly Abū Jahl vowed to stop the Prophet ﷺ from praying, while ʿUtbah and al-Walīd offered marriage and wealth if he gave up his mission. Ayah 24 answers: obey none of them.
explained: Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ that He is the one sending down the Quran, piece by piece. So be patient with Allah’s decree, keep delivering the message, and don’t obey the āthim, the sinner, or the kafūr, the denier. Strength comes from remembering Allah morning and evening and praying long at night.

The real reason for denial: they love al-ʿājilah, the quick world, and ignore a heavy Day ahead. Allah made them and firmed their frames; He can replace or remake them. This surah is a reminder. Anyone can take a path to Allah, yet no one wills except by His will, and He knows who deserves guidance.
teaches: The Quran is from Allah, so hold on to it.
Don’t give in to pressure against the truth.
Worship, especially at night, gives strength to be patient.
Love of this world blinds people to the Hereafter.
Choose the path to Allah, and ask Him for it.
sections.hook: Three commands in a row: be patient (24), remember (25), prostrate and glorify (26). Shāʾa (to will) repeats through 28–31. Sabīl returns in 29, echoing ayah 3.

groups.text: There was a long time when man was nothing worth mentioning.
Allah made man from a mixed drop to test him, gave him hearing and sight, and showed him the way.
For the disbelievers: chains, iron collars and a blazing Fire.
The righteous drink a cup mixed with camphor, from a spring they can make flow wherever they like.
They keep their vows and fear a Day whose evil spreads everywhere.
They feed the poor, the orphan and the captive for Allah alone, wanting no thanks, fearing a grim Day.
Allah shields them from that Day, gives them radiance and joy, and rewards their patience with a garden and silk.
They recline on couches, with no heat or cold, close shade, and fruit hanging within reach.
Servants bring silver vessels clear as glass, filled to just the right measure.
They drink a cup mixed with ginger, from a spring called Salsabīl.
Ageless youths serve them like scattered pearls; everywhere is bliss and a great kingdom.
Green silk, silver bracelets and a pure drink from their Lord. “This is your reward; your effort is appreciated.”
Allah sent the Quran down in stages, so be patient and obey no sinner or denier.
Remember your Lord morning and evening, and prostrate and glorify Him through the long night.
The deniers love this passing world and ignore a heavy Day. Allah made them and can replace them.
This is a reminder: whoever wills takes a path to Allah, but only by His will. Then mercy, or punishment.

1.explain: Hal atā: a question with an obvious answer, “indeed there was”. A long stretch of time when man was nothing worth mentioning: either Adam as a clay form before the soul, or each person before birth.

2.explain: Nuṭfah amshāj: a drop mixed from the man’s and woman’s fluids, then changed stage by stage. Nabtalīhi: to test him. So Allah gave him hearing and sight, to use in obedience or disobedience.

3.explain: Hadaynāhu as-sabīl: Allah made the way clear through messengers and books, showing the path of good and of evil. Man is then either shākir, a grateful believer, or kafūr, an ungrateful denier.

4.explain: For the deniers: salāsil, chains to drag them; aghlāl, iron collars binding hands to necks; and saʿīr, a blazing Fire. One ayah, and then the passage turns to the righteous.

5.explain: Al-abrār: the righteous, good in heart and deed. They drink a cup mixed with kāfūr: cool and fragrant, with none of worldly camphor’s faults. Or Kāfūr is the name of a spring.

6.explain: ʿAynan: a spring that never runs dry. Yufajjirūnahā tafjīrā: they make it gush wherever they wish, to their gardens, homes and palaces.

7.explain: Yūfūna bin-nadhr: they keep their vows. If they keep promises they chose to make, they keep Allah’s obligations even more. They fear a Day whose evil is mustaṭīr, spreading everywhere.

8.explain: ʿAlā ḥubbihi: they give food while loving and needing it themselves (or out of love for Allah), to the miskīn (poor), the yatīm (orphan) and the asīr (captive), even a non-Muslim captive.
8.why: Reportedly a poor man, then an orphan, then a captive asked the Prophet ﷺ for food. He had none, so each went to an Anṣārī whose wife said: “Feed him.” Other reports name different people; the ayah covers all the righteous.

9.explain: Li-wajhillāh: only for Allah’s pleasure. No payment, no praise. They may not even say it aloud; Allah knows it is in their hearts and praises them for it.

10.explain: ʿAbūsan qamṭarīrā: a grim, long, distressing Day that makes faces frown and scowl. Their generosity comes from fearing it.

11.explain: Allah shields them from the evil they feared, and gives them naḍrah, radiance on their faces, and surūr, joy in their hearts: beauty outside and inside.

12.explain: Bimā ṣabarū: for their patience in obeying Allah, avoiding sin and accepting hardship. Their reward: a garden with every delight, and silk to wear.

13.explain: Muttakiʾīn ʿalā al-arāʾik: reclining at ease on couches under canopies. No shams, burning sun, and no zamharīr, bitter cold: one pleasant climate, always.

14.explain: Its shade is close over them, and its quṭūf, fruit clusters, are lowered within reach, whether they stand, sit or lie down.

15.explain: Servants go around with vessels of silver and akwāb, cups without handles, that are clear like qawārīr, glass.

16.explain: Qawārīr min fiḍḍah: silver, yet see-through like glass, with nothing like it in this world. Qaddarūhā taqdīrā: each is filled to exactly the amount that satisfies, no more, no less.

17.explain: A cup mixed with zanjabīl, ginger, a flavour the Arabs loved. Camphor cools and ginger warms, and neither is like its worldly version.

18.explain: ʿAynan fīhā: from a spring there named Salsabīl, so called because it is smooth and flows easily down the throat.

19.explain: Wildān mukhalladūn: youths who never age or change. Spread out as they serve, their beauty looks like luʾluʾ manthūr, scattered pearls.

20.explain: Wherever you look there: naʿīm, bliss beyond description, and mulk kabīr, a vast kingdom. Even the lowest in Paradise is given the like of this world and ten times more.

21.explain: ʿĀliyahum: over them green sundus, fine silk, and istabraq, brocade. Silver bracelets (gold elsewhere). Sharāb ṭahūr: a pure drink that cleanses their hearts of envy and grudges.

22.explain: Inna hādhā kāna lakum jazāʾ: this is your reward. Saʿyukum mashkūrā: your effort is appreciated. Allah repays a little effort with endless bliss.

23.explain: Innā naḥnu nazzalnā: it is Allah Himself who sent the Quran down, not anyone else. Tanzīlā: in stages, ayah by ayah, not all at once.

24.explain: Fa-ṣbir li-ḥukmi rabbik: be patient with Allah’s decree and keep delivering the message. Obey no āthim, sinner in deeds, or kafūr, denier at heart, whoever it is.
24.why: Reportedly Abū Jahl threatened to step on the Prophet’s ﷺ neck if he saw him praying. Another report: ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah offered his daughter in marriage, and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah offered wealth, if he would abandon his mission.

25.explain: Remember your Lord’s name bukratan wa aṣīlā, at the start and end of the day: the prayers of those times, and remembrance and glorification.

26.explain: In the night, prostrate to Him (the evening prayers), and glorify Him through a long night: voluntary night prayer. Worship is what strengthens patience.

27.explain: These deniers love al-ʿājilah, the fast-passing world, and leave warāʾahum, ahead of them (or behind their backs), a heavy Day they neither believe in nor work for.

28.explain: Shadadnā asrahum: We made their frames strong, with joints and sinews. The One who made them can remake them for the Resurrection, or replace them with others like them.

29.explain: Hādhihi tadhkirah: this surah is a reminder. Whoever wills can take a sabīl, a path, to his Lord through obedience. The truth is clear, and the choice is given.

30.explain: But you can only will what Allah wills. He is ʿAlīm, knowing who deserves guidance, and Ḥakīm, wise in whom He guides and whom He leaves astray.

31.explain: He admits whom He wills into His mercy, His Paradise. For aẓ-ẓālimīn, who chose ruin over guidance, He has prepared a painful punishment.
